amendments.rule: An English function word the ASV supplies for an adverbial accusative belongs to the noun whose case-function licenses it — *as a bird*, *to your mountain* — and is never `added`. **An appositional or measure nominal the ASV introduces with a supplied preposition is read the same way.** Where a noun or numeral stands in the clause with no preposition and no object marker on it, and the ASV writes an *of* or a *for* before it to state what that nominal contributes, the word is that nominal's own rendering: `אֹרֶךְ חֲמִשָּׁה וְעֶשְׂרִים אֶלֶף` → *the length ... of five and twenty thousand*, `תֹּכֶן אֶחָד` → *of one measure*, `לַאֲחֻזָּה עֶשְׂרִים לְשָׁכֹת` → *for a possession ..., for twenty chambers*, `חַטָּאת שְׂעִיר עִזִּים` → *a he goat ... for a sin offering*. It goes to the word it stands before, which is the noun or numeral opening that phrase, and the unit still heads on the word carrying the lexeme under rules 24 and 31; the supplied preposition is never the head. **A preposition standing elsewhere in the clause that has already taken an English word of its own does not make such a word a surplus.** Rule 52's count governs two English words offered to one morpheme, and here each phrase has a rendering of its own, so a written `לְ` rendered *for a possession* does not silence the *for* the ASV writes before the phrase standing beside it. **But the noun must be present.** Where the ASV supplies the head noun as well as the function word, no morpheme is there to carry either, and the whole supplied phrase is its own `added` unit under rule 30: `חֲמֵשׁ מֵאוֹת בַּחֲמֵשׁ מֵאוֹת` → *five hundred* ***in length*** *by five hundred* ***in breadth*** supplies both the preposition and the dimension noun in a clause whose Hebrew names neither, exactly as the italic ***reeds*** of `חֲמִשָּׁה וְעֶשְׂרִים אֶלֶף` supplies a measure noun. Test by subtraction as rules 16 and 31 do: drop the English and ask whether a Hebrew noun standing in the clause has lost the relation it bears, or whether what has gone is a noun the Hebrew never wrote. An ASV italic on such a word corroborates it either way and decides nothing, by rule 7. **And a bare noun that completes a predicate's own valency is not an adverbial accusative at all.** Where a verb or a predicate adjective governs a bare noun as its complement — no preposition and no object marker on it — and the English predicate can reach that complement only through a preposition the ASV has written, that word answers to the predicate's valency and joins the predicate's unit under rule 44, while the noun keeps its own English: `מָלֵאתָ` → *thou art full* ***of*** *the judgment* and `מָלֵא דָשֶׁן` → *would be full* ***of*** *fatness* both give the *of* to `מָלֵא`, headed on *full*, and leave `דִין` and `דֶשֶׁן` their own words. Decide it by asking whether the ASV had a relation to choose: where the English predicate admits no other word before such a complement — *full of* is the only way English writes it — the preposition is the predicate's, and where the word states what the noun contributes to the clause and another would have served, this rule governs and the word is the noun's, as it does for `יָזֹקּוּ מָטָר` → *distil* ***in*** *rain* and `כַּבִּיר כֹּחַ` → *mighty* ***in*** *strength*. Read the English predicate rather than where the noun stands, since Hebrew writes such a complement before its predicate as readily as after it, and JOB.36.16 and JOB.36.17 are the two shapes in one chapter.
amendments.why: Rule 33's first sentences reach any supplied function word before a bare noun, and rule 44's limit sends a predicate's complement back to rule 44 without saying how to tell the two apart. JOB.36's two `מָלֵא` clauses were read under the two rules and split, so the qualification belongs in rule 33, which is what a pass looking at a supplied preposition reads first. It allocates nothing rule 44 does not already claim in its bare-object clause, and it ratifies the chapter's `מָלֵא` patch while leaving *mighty in strength* and *distil in rain* where rule 33 has them.

conventions: `מָלֵא` with a bare accusative of material: the supplied *of* is the predicate's under rule 44, never the noun's under rule 33. `דִין־רָשָׁע מָלֵאתָ` (36.17) → *thou art full of the judgment* and `מָלֵא דָשֶׁן` (36.16) → *would be full of fatness* both give *of* to `מָלֵא`, headed on *full*, and leave the noun its own word; 36.16 was patched to match. Word order does not change the reading. An adjunct accusative in the same chapter keeps its own supplied preposition, as `כַּבִּיר כֹּחַ` → *mighty in strength* (36.5) and `יָזֹקּוּ מָטָר` → *distil in rain* (36.27) do, because there the ASV had a relation to choose and *full* does not.

A subject pronoun the ASV supplies for a clause that writes no subject morpheme joins the predicate word whose agreement it realizes, and is `added` only where no morpheme in the clause carries person, gender or number for it. The predicate adjective `כַּבִּיר` takes *He is* (36.5, the subject gapped from the first line's `אֵל`) and the passive participle `אֲסוּרִים` takes *they be* (36.8), while the *thou* of `לֹא בְצָר` → *that thou be not in distress* (36.19) is `added`, rule 49 having given that clause's copula to the `בְ`, which agrees with nothing. Rule 20's copula goes to the predicate in all three, and the competing readings are named in each verse's notes.

report: One real split. `מָלֵא` with a bare accusative of material was analysed two ways: JOB.36.17 `דִין־רָשָׁע מָלֵאתָ` → *thou art full of the judgment* gives the supplied *of* to the verb under rule 44, while JOB.36.16 `מָלֵא דָשֶׁן` → *would be full of fatness* gave it to the noun under rule 33. Both nouns are bare — no preposition, no object marker — so the only difference is that one stands before its predicate and one after, which the contract nowhere makes decisive. JOB.36.16 is patched to rule 44, whose own text names an *of* case (`תְּבַצְּעִי רֵעַיִךְ` → *hast greedily gained of thy neighbors*); JOB.36.17 stands unchanged.

Candidate table cleared. The 36 groups are the ASV rendering one word differently: the waw connectives (*and*, *But*, *Then*, *also*, *Or*), the `בְּ`/`לְ`/`עַל`/`מִן` prepositions, the article, `כִּי` and the negatives all follow what the ASV wrote. `אַף` shows three treatments only because 36.16 alone has a waw before it, fused to *Yea* under rule 30, while 36.29 and 36.33 have none. `מִן` + `רָחוֹק` is split at 36.3 (*from afar*) and fused at 36.25 (*afar off*) because the ASV writes two ownable words in one and not in the other.

The `added` inventory was read end to end (16 units), since the table is blind to it. Supplied object pronouns (*him* 36.11, *him* 36.26, *it* 36.25), supplied object nouns (*any* 36.5, *the mark* 36.32, *on thee* 36.17), supplied possessives (*their* 36.6, *thy* 36.19, *his* 36.32), supplied connectives (*And* 36.8, 36.28), the supplied relative *Which* 36.27 and the gapped lexical verb *perisheth* 36.14 are uniformly `added`. The one folded case — *the life* joining `יְחַיֶּה` at 36.6 — is licensed by rule 44's lexeme test, and 36.32's *it* goes to a suffix that is present. No inconsistency there.

Supplied subject pronouns are a boundary rather than a split, and are recorded as a convention instead of patched: 36.5 gives *He is* to the predicate adjective `כַּבִּיר` and 36.8 gives *they be* to the passive participle `אֲסוּרִים`, both of which agree with the pronoun written, while 36.19 leaves *thou* `added` because rule 49 hands that clause's copula to the `בְ` of `בְצָר`, a morpheme carrying no person, gender or number for a pronoun to realize. Rule 20's copula goes to the predicate in all three.

BSB: none of the ten disagreements is an error. Seven are prepositions the ASV's recasting leaves nothing to say (rule 40: dative `לְ` as a bare object at 36.2, 36.3, 36.9; `עַל`/`אֶל` with a promoted object at 36.21, 36.23, 36.32), one is the second waw of 36.7 for which the ASV writes no connective after *But*, and two are the paragogic nuns of 36.8 and 36.10 (rule 32). All are the documented convention difference, and no accepted edge was moved to improve the rate.

Also reviewed and left: the head of 36.14's `נַפְשָׁם` → *They*, taken on `נֶפֶשׁ` by rule 6's deterministic anchor. The suffix is a defensible competing head under rule 6's carve-out, since a bare Sp3mp is ordinarily *they*, but the English recasts the possessive phrase as a subject pronoun rather than writing the suffix's own rendering, and the verse note already names the alternative. Outside the cross-verse remit, so unchanged.
